strengths: Addresses critical question for mechanistic interpretability: whether SAE features represent learned computations or statistical artifacts from data
Comprehensive experimental design across multiple model sizes (70M-6.9B), layers, and well-designed controls including Step-0 and random embedding baseline
Robust to hyperparameter selection (Figure 11) and evaluates across multiple metrics (AUROC, explained variance, cosine similarity, L1 norm, CE loss)
Clever use of token distribution entropy to quantify feature abstraction level, providing quantitative evidence that random models learn simpler, more token-specific features
Provides theoretical grounding through toy models (Section 4) demonstrating superposition preservation/amplification and validation on real embeddings
Well-written with clear motivation, reproducible methodology, and detailed experimental setup; advocates for concrete methodological improvement (random model controls)
weaknesses: Core mechanistic question remains unresolved: Section 4.2 finds evidence both that random NNs preserve and amplify superposition, with only modest differences shown (Figure 6). Conclusions deferred to future work significantly limit explanatory value

Limited scope of auto-interpretability evaluation: only fuzzing method tested (not simulation scoring), only 100 features sampled per variant, and no human evaluation. Reliance on single metric raises concerns about whether findings generalize to other evaluation approaches

Implications somewhat overstated: main finding is specific to fuzzing auto-interpretability metric; other metrics (CE loss, feature abstraction) DO distinguish trained from random models. Title suggests broader failure of SAEs than results warrant

Incomplete analysis of embedding effects: 'Randomized excl. embeddings' performs better than Step-0, suggesting pre-trained embeddings carry structure. This crucial observation is under-explored and somewhat contradicts the superposition-in-input-data hypothesis

Limited generalization: only Pythia models tested for main results (though across sizes), only transformer residual stream, only RedPajama dataset. Results may not transfer to other architectures or datasets
No statistical rigor reporting: lacks confidence intervals, significance tests, or analysis of variance across random seeds, making it difficult to assess finding stability
Token entropy metric is acknowledged as indirect proxy for abstraction; unclear whether it captures what practitioners care about or could reflect other factors
Missing key ablations: why 'Randomized excl. embeddings' outperforms Step-0? What if parameter norms controlled differently? Why not evaluate simulation-based scoring alongside fuzzing?

strengths: Addresses an important methodological question for mechanistic interpretability research regarding whether SAE features reflect learned computations
Comprehensive experimental design with multiple model variants and scales (70M-6.9B parameters), providing solid empirical coverage
Novel token distribution entropy metric successfully differentiates trained and randomized models, showing qualitative differences in feature complexity
Thoughtful toy model analysis (Section 4) providing mathematical intuition for why superposition might be preserved through neural network transformations
Uses open-source tools and clearly describes implementations, supporting reproducibility
Clear presentation of empirical results through ROC curves and metric comparisons across multiple model sizes
weaknesses: Mechanism understanding is explicitly deferred to future work despite this being central to the paper's core claim, undermining mechanistic interpretability contribution

Main finding relies heavily on a single auto-interpretability method (fuzzing) that itself may be problematic—the fact that random models score similarly suggests potential method limitations rather than SAE flaws
Critical empirical observation (randomized models outperform Step-0 initialization) is speculated upon but not rigorously investigated, representing a significant gap in understanding

Overstated framing: title suggests successful interpretation of random models, but evidence shows only superficial pattern-finding with poor cross-entropy loss and token-specific (non-abstract) features
Limited positive contributions: identifies problems but offers minimal actionable guidance for practitioners or the field beyond vague recommendation to use null models
Incomplete experimental evaluation: relies on single auto-interpretability method without testing simulation scoring; no intervention-based validation; limited SAE architecture coverage (TopK only)
Weak statistical rigor: only 100 features sampled, no error bars or confidence intervals, no significance testing across variants
Toy model analysis (Section 4) uses unjustified parameter choices and shows only marginal differences between superposed and Gaussian outputs, with authors acknowledging results are inconclusive

Missing crucial ablations: no tests of steering/ablation effectiveness for random models, no investigation of whether results generalize beyond Pythia, no systematic analysis of whether input data properties vs. architecture drive the phenomenon
The 'control' variant (random embeddings at inference) lacks theoretical justification—unclear why this is the appropriate baseline comparison

strengths: Addresses critical methodological question for mechanistic interpretability: whether SAEs capture learned structure or statistical artifacts
Comprehensive experimental design across five model sizes with rigorous controls and systematic per-layer analysis
Novel token distribution entropy analysis reveals important abstractness dimension missed by auto-interpretability metrics
Multi-faceted evaluation using reconstruction metrics (explained variance, cosine similarity, L1), auto-interpretability scores, and CE loss provides convincing evidence
Robust hyperparameter sweep demonstrates stability of findings across expansion factors and sparsity parameters
Clear writing with good presentation, full reproducibility details, and open-source implementations
Important cautionary finding for the mechanistic interpretability community about limitations of current evaluation practices
weaknesses: Mechanistic explanation is incomplete and explicitly deferred to future work; two hypotheses presented but only partially validated, especially for word embeddings
Limited scope: only tested on Pythia models with TopK SAEs; would benefit from other model families, SAE architectures, or datasets
Insufficient interrogation of auto-interpretability metrics themselves; paper relies on LLM-based explanations whose validity is debatable, without exploring sensitivity to LLM choice
No concrete solutions proposed; recommendations are generic ('develop better techniques'), and token distribution entropy is directional but incomplete
Core finding is somewhat expected given prior work on random network structure; novelty is in systematic documentation rather than conceptual surprise
Cross-entropy loss results (Figure 3, row 5) showing trained SAEs improve performance while random models degrade it—a crucial distinction—deserve more prominent analysis
Limited systematic analysis of feature content beyond entropy; examples are cherry-picked rather than comprehensively characterized

strengths: Important negative result demonstrating that common SAE evaluation metrics (especially auto-interpretability scores) fail to distinguish trained from random transformers, challenging fundamental evaluation practices in mechanistic interpretability
Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation across model sizes (70M-6.9B), multiple randomization schemes, and diverse metrics with proper uncertainty quantification and robustness checks
Well-designed methodology with clever baseline conditions (particularly the control variant) and multiple evaluation approaches that strengthen validity of findings
Clear presentation with effective motivation, well-organized results, and extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Thoughtful analysis including toy models exploring mechanistic hypotheses and proposal of token distribution entropy as a more discriminative metric
Significant practical contribution to the field by establishing the need for randomized baselines in SAE evaluation and highlighting limitations of aggregate metrics
weaknesses: Incomplete mechanistic understanding: paper identifies that random models achieve similar metrics but doesn't definitively explain why, with toy models demonstrating plausibility but explicitly deferring conclusions to future work
Limited solutions provided: token distribution entropy proposed only as 'proof-of-concept' without systematic validation across all configurations or rigorous comparison with alternatives
Narrow scope: limited to Pythia models and RedPajama dataset; unclear generalization to other SAE architectures, model families, or domains
Insufficient practical guidance: paper doesn't clearly advise practitioners on when/whether to use SAEs or provide validated alternatives for safe deployment
Incomplete evaluation of proposed solution: entropy metric shown qualitatively but lacks systematic quantitative validation, statistical significance testing, and analysis of when it works
Gap between trained and random models narrows for larger models (6.9B), suggesting severity of issue may be limited at scale, but this trend not thoroughly investigated
Simplified toy models in Section 4 may not capture real transformer dynamics, limiting explanatory power for understanding the phenomenon
Code availability not mentioned; some implementation details missing (exact prompts, complete hyperparameter specifications)

strengths: Important sanity check: Demonstrates that standard SAE metrics fail to distinguish trained from random models, raising critical questions about mechanistic interpretability evaluation
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Tests across multiple model sizes (70M-7B), randomization schemes, evaluation metrics, and hyperparameter settings with good experimental design
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with clear motivation, systematic methodology, and honest discussion of findings
Proper experimental rigor: Includes multiple random seeds (for some experiments), ablations on hyperparameters and training data, and addresses reproducibility concerns
Proposed alternative metric: Token distribution entropy offers a partial solution that better distinguishes trained from random models in some settings
Extensive supplementary material: Comprehensive appendices support reproducibility with implementation details and feature examples
weaknesses: Limited novelty and primarily negative result: The paper identifies a problem but provides only an incomplete solution. Lacks the depth of mechanistic understanding or constructive contributions expected for top-tier acceptance

Incomplete mechanistic explanation: Section 4 remains speculative about which mechanism (preservation vs. amplification of superposition) dominates, without definitive resolution between competing hypotheses

Missing critical downstream task evaluation: No evaluation of whether SAE features from trained models actually work better for mechanistic interpretability tasks (intervention, steering, counterfactual analysis) than random models

Weak proposed solution: Token distribution entropy is a simple statistical property, not a mechanistic interpretability measure. Lacks evaluation of whether entropy-based discrimination correlates with actual interpretability quality
Limited scope: Only tested on language models (Pythia), single dataset (RedPajama), specific SAE architecture (k-sparse R=64,k=32), and one explanation model (Llama-3.1-70B). Generalizability unclear

Reproducibility concerns: Auto-interpretability scores depend heavily on explanation model choice with minimal ablation; most experiments use single random seeds; unclear if differences are statistically significant
Philosophical ambiguity: Paper treats 'learned' vs. 'random' as binary but doesn't resolve what definitively makes a feature 'legitimately learned' vs. reflecting architectural/statistical artifacts
Incomplete analysis of alternatives: No investigation of combining metrics, other sparsity-inducing methods, or whether problem affects non-SAE interpretability approaches
Token entropy metric under-explored: Why is entropy the right measure of 'abstractness'? Relationship to interpretability quality is assumed rather than demonstrated

strengths: Important sanity check for mechanistic interpretability research showing auto-interpretability metrics fail to distinguish trained from random models
Comprehensive experimental design across multiple model sizes, randomization schemes, and evaluation metrics with strong robustness checks
Well-executed empirical work with excellent reproducibility (public models/data, uncertainty quantification, multiple random seeds, hyperparameter ablations)
Theoretical grounding through toy models demonstrating why random networks might produce interpretable-looking features via superposition
Clear presentation and well-designed visualizations (Figures 1-2) effectively communicating the main findings
Proposes token distribution entropy as a concrete alternative metric that better captures feature abstractness
Extensive appendices with detailed analyses, feature dashboards, and qualitative examples demonstrating thorough investigation
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty - primarily applies existing metrics to a new comparison setting; token entropy is relatively straightforward
Incomplete solution to identified problem - token entropy is acknowledged as ad-hoc and indirect proxy, lacks rigorous validation against ground truth abstractness definitions
Insufficient mechanistic understanding - competing hypotheses about superposition remain unresolved with causal mechanisms deferred to future work
Scope limitations - only Pythia models tested, only language modeling, single LLM for explanation generation; generalization unclear
Limited practical guidance - paper identifies problems but doesn't clearly advise practitioners on solutions or implications for published work
Incomplete qualitative analysis - systematic feature comparison relegated to appendix; main text would benefit from more detailed examples
Insufficient explanation of metric failure modes - doesn't determine whether failures stem from LLM limitations, architectural biases, or fundamental approach flaws
Missing important comparisons with other mechanistic interpretability evaluation approaches and recent work on validating interpretability metrics
Limited discussion of implications for the field - unclear whether auto-interpretability should be abandoned, when it remains valid, or how to rebuild confidence in SAE-based findings
